Links: [{"title":"Docker Scout health scores | Docker Docs","url":"https://docs.docker.com/scout/policy/scores/"},{"title":"\"No outdated base images\" on `docker scout` · Issue #58 · KEINOS/Dockerfile_of_SQLite3","url":"https://github.com/KEINOS/Dockerfile_of_SQLite3/issues/58"},{"title":"How to Use Docker Scout to Analyze Image Vulnerabilities","url":"https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-08-how-to-use-docker-scout-to-analyze-image-vulnerabilities/view"},{"title":"Docker scout is picking up incorrect base image - Docker Scout - Docker Community Forums","url":"https://forums.docker.com/t/docker-scout-is-picking-up-incorrect-base-image/151537"},{"title":"Image Analyze can't finish · Issue #72 · docker/scout-cli","url":"https://github.com/docker/scout-cli/issues/72"},{"title":"Docker Scout image analysis | Docker Docs","url":"https://docs.docker.com/scout/explore/analysis/"},{"title":"Docker Scout in the UI Cannot Analyse Image Which Has Already Been Analysed via Command Line · Issue #14958 · docker/for-win","url":"https://github.com/docker/for-win/issues/14958"},{"title":"Docker scout is misreading base image version number · Issue #84 · docker/scout-cli","url":"https://github.com/docker/scout-cli/issues/84"},{"title":"Docker Scout quickstart | Docker Docs","url":"https://docs.docker.com/scout/quickstart/"}]

The exact phrasing you're searching for comes from the **Docker Scout health scores** documentation page (docs.docker.com/scout/policy/scores/), where it describes when an image gets an **N/A score** rather than a failed analysis per se.

## The N/A score conditions

Images can be assigned an N/A score, which can happen when: the image is larger than 4GB (compressed size); the image architecture is not linux/amd64 or linux/arm64; or the image is too old and does not have fresh data for evaluation.

## Remediation guidance

The docs give direct fixes for two of these: if the image has an unsupported architecture, rebuild the image for a supported architecture; if the image is too old, push a new tag to trigger a fresh evaluation.

## Related context

- Health scores are derived from policy evaluation: each policy is assigned a points value based on its type, compliant images are awarded that policy type's points, and the health score is calculated as the percentage of points achieved relative to the total possible points.
- Health scores are calculated for new images pushed to Docker Hub after the feature is enabled, and in addition to individual image scores (per tag or digest), each repository receives a health score based on the latest pushed tag.

The size/architecture limits also surface in the CLI as a generic error — users have reported the message that an image couldn't be analyzed because it may have an unsupported architecture, or exceed the maximum size, which was hit on a 6.2 GB image.

Note that a *failed policy status* is a different thing from an N/A score — that's reported separately, e.g. "Policy status FAILED (4/7 policies met, 2 missing data)", where "missing data" typically means Docker Scout uses provenance attestations to find out the base image version and they weren't present.

Primary source: https://docs.docker.com/scout/policy/scores/

Here's what the search turned up on scanner options that emit SARIF for GitHub code scanning:

## Both major open-source scanners support the SARIF → GitHub pipelineBoth integrate well. Trivy has an official GitHub Action (aquasecurity/trivy-action) and Docker images. Grype has an official GitHub Action (anchore/scan-action@v7) and Docker images. Both output SARIF for GitHub/GitLab code scanning and support severity-based build gating. The integration experience is comparable. Both support severity-based exit codes for build gating.

The typical wiring is a two-step job: scanner produces SARIF, then `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3` ingests it. With Trivy, you set `format: 'sarif'` and `output: 'trivy-results.sarif'`, then upload with `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3`; after uploading, findings appear in the Security tab under "Code scanning alerts," with each vulnerability linking to its CVE entry with remediation guidance. For Grype, `anchore/scan-action@v7` takes `image`, `fail-build`, and `severity-cutoff` inputs and then feeds a SARIF report to the same upload step.

## Trade-offs between the twoTrivy is the broad all-in-one scanner — one binary scans container images, filesystems, Git repos, IaC, Kubernetes, secrets, and licenses, and generates SBOMs — while Grype is the focused container and filesystem vulnerability scanner that pairs with Syft for an SBOM-first workflow. Grype is known for precise version matching with low false positives thanks to Anchore's curated grype-db; Trivy's broader feed mix can surface more findings, occasionally at the cost of extra noise on edge-case packages.Trivy uses Aqua's own vulnerability database (trivy-db) plus a separate Java database (trivy-java-db), while Grype aggregates data from NVD, GitHub Security Advisories, Alpine SecDB, Debian Security Tracker, Red Hat Security Data, Ubuntu, Amazon Linux, and Oracle Linux. Both databases update daily.

On integration depth: Trivy offers a native GitHub Actions action, GitLab template, Jenkins plugin, and pre-built integrations broadly, with SARIF output supported and CLI use in any pipeline, whereas Grype has a clean CLI, GitHub Actions action, and SARIF output, but less native integration depth than Trivy. Trivy's Kubernetes operator (trivy-operator) runs continuous scans inside clusters, which Grype does not offer.

## Caveat on your windows/amd64 question

The results didn't directly address Windows container image support (`windows/amd64` layers, or scanning Windows base images / KB-level patch detection) for either tool — that specific capability question isn't answered by these sources. Worth noting the practical constraint the workflow examples imply: the sample Grype and Trivy jobs run on `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` with a `docker build`, so scanning Windows images generally requires either a `windows-` runner for the build or pulling the image by reference from a Linux runner. If you need a definitive answer on Windows OS-package vulnerability matching, checking the Grype and Trivy docs directly for supported package ecosystems would be the reliable next step.

One risk-reducing option the sources mention: Grype provides another option with different detection capabilities, and running multiple scanners catches issues that one might miss — since both upload SARIF to the same Security tab, running them in parallel is low-cost.

input.content:
# Research: flutter-windows is not analyzed by Docker Scout (issue #506)

Explored 2026-08-09. Tracking issue: <https://github.com/gmeligio/flutter-docker-image/issues/506>

## Verdict up front

The issue asks a yes/no question — "verify whether Scout produces meaningful
output for the Windows image" — and the answer is **no, on three independent
grounds**. Scout is the wrong tool for `flutter-windows`, and no drop-in
replacement exists either. Adding `flutter-windows` to the `record-image`
matrix would produce a red or empty leg, not coverage.

But the issue's framing ("the same matrix-omission pattern as
`update-description`") is the more important half, and it is correct. #506 is
the third known instance of one structural defect, and a fourth was found
during this exploration. The defect is worth fixing even though *this*
symptom turns out to be a documentation task rather than a code task.

## Context

`record-image` (`.github/workflows/release.yml:227-276`) runs
`docker/scout-action` with `command: environment, cves` against
`registry://<owner>/<name>:<tag>`, then uploads SARIF to GitHub code scanning
with a per-image `category` (`release.yml:273-275`). Its matrix
(`release.yml:241-243`) lists `flutter-android` and `flutter-web`; it declares
`needs: release-linux` (`release.yml:234`).

```
  push: refs/tags/*
        │
        ├──▶ release-linux ──────────┐  matrix [android, web]   release.yml:35-39
        │     (NO outputs:)          │
        │                            │
        └──▶ release-windows ─┐      │  uses windows-image.yml   release.yml:123-140
              (NO outputs:)   │      │
                              │      │
        ┌─────────────────────┴──────┴──────────┬──────────────┐
        ▼                    ▼                  ▼              ▼
  verify-published    update-description   record-image   create-github-release
  needs:[linux,       needs: release-linux needs:         needs: release-linux
         windows]                          release-linux
   :158-161            :193-195             :241-243        :285
  [android,web,WIN]   [android,web] ✗win   [android,web] ✗win
        ✓ correct         ✗ gap #2            ✗ ISSUE #506
```

Every one of those four post-publish jobs re-states the image set by hand.
`verify-published` is the only one that got it right — and it did so for a
documented reason, in a comment that is effectively a post-mortem of #506
written before #506 was filed (`release.yml:143-147`):

> "Did it publish?" is read from the registry by an anonymous pull, never
> inferred from which release job succeeded — that coupling is what let this
> job drift before.

That lesson was learned once and applied to exactly one job.

## Findings

### 1. Scout cannot analyze this image — three independent disqualifiers

**(a) Architecture.** Docker's health-scores page states an image is scored
N/A when "the image architecture is not linux/amd64 or linux/arm64", with the
remediation "rebuild the image for a supported architecture"
(<https://docs.docker.com/scout/policy/scores/>). Verified against the
actually-published artifact — pulling the config blob for
`docker.io/gmeligio/flutter-windows:3.44.9` from the registry API:

```
os: windows    arch: amd64    os.version: 10.0.26100.32690
```

Not a rebuildable property: Windows containers are `windows/amd64` by
construction.

**(b) Size.** The same page sets an N/A threshold at 4 GB compressed (the
analysis page separately documents a 10 GB uncompressed platform limit —
<https://docs.docker.com/scout/explore/analysis/>). Measured from the
published manifest: **37 layers, 5.90 GB compressed**, with the servercore
base alone at 1.42 GB. Over the limit before Flutter is even added.

**(c) No advisory data or package inventory even if (a) and (b) were waived.**
Scout's advisory sources
(<https://docs.docker.com/scout/deep-dive/advisory-db-sources/>) list 23
feeds — AlmaLinux, Alpine, Amazon Linux, Chainguard, Debian, Oracle, Photon,
RedHat, Rocky, SUSE, Ubuntu, Wolfi, plus language ecosystems. **No Microsoft
/ MSRC / Windows feed appears.** Supported package ecosystems are `.NET`, Go,
Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, RPM, Ruby, `alpm`, `apk`, `deb`, GitHub
packages — every OS-level format is a Linux one.

This last point is the deepest one, because it survives any change of tool.
Scanners are SBOM-driven, and an SBOM needs a package database to read.
Look at what `windows.Dockerfile` actually installs:

| Component | Install mechanism | `windows.Dockerfile` |
|---|---|---|
| Git | MinGit `.zip`, unpacked | `:20` |
| Flutter SDK | `git clone` | `:42` |
| VS Build Tools (VCTools, CMake, Win11 SDK) | VS installer `.exe` | `:74` |
| Pester (test stage) | `InstallPester.ps1` | `:135-139` |

Zero of these are registered with any package manager. There is no
`/var/lib/dpkg/status` analogue to parse — and even the base OS ships its
patch state as Windows Update KB records, which no SBOM cataloger models.
A scanner pointed at this image finds an empty inventory, so an empty report
is the *correct* result, not a bug.

### 2. No Windows-capable replacement exists in the open-source scanner space

The issue's fallback ("use a Windows-capable scanner instead") was checked
and does not have an answer today:

- **Trivy** — the supported-OS coverage table
  (<https://trivy.dev/latest/docs/coverage/os/>) lists ~22 distributions.
  Windows / Server Core / Nano Server has no row, footnote, or nav entry.
  Trivy's docs also state it only covers "official packages provided by
  vendors" via a package manager.
- **Grype / Syft** (<https://github.com/anchore/grype>) — Grype delegates
  cataloging to Syft, so any Syft gap propagates. Syft's catalogers cover
  Linux package formats and language manifests; no MSI, CBS servicing stack,
  or KB-level cataloger exists.

The only tools that model Windows patch state are Microsoft's own (Defender
for Cloud registry scanning), and Microsoft documents that runtime
vulnerability assessment "isn't supported for container images running on
Windows nodes"
(<https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/agentless-vulnerability-assessment-azure>).
Nothing here plugs into a `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif` step against a
public GHCR/Docker Hub image.

**What actually governs Windows base-image CVE posture** is the base image
tag, not a scanner. Microsoft rebuilds Windows base images monthly on the
second Tuesday, plus out-of-band for critical CVEs
(<https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/virtualization/windowscontainers/manage-containers/container-base-images>).
`windows.Dockerfile:3` pins `servercore:ltsc2025` by digest — so the
project's real Windows CVE control is *how promptly that digest is bumped*,
which is a Renovate concern, not a Scout concern.

```
  What the issue assumed              What is actually true
  ─────────────────────────           ─────────────────────────
  Scout ──▶ flutter-windows           Scout ──╳ windows/amd64 (arch)
     │                                        ╳ 5.90 GB       (size)
     ▼                                        ╳ no MSRC feed  (data)
  SARIF ──▶ code scanning
                                      CVE posture governed by:
                                      digest bump of servercore:ltsc2025
                                      (windows.Dockerfile:3) ──▶ Renovate
```

### 3. The real defect: the image set is enumerated 12+ times and nothing owns it

This is the finding that outlives #506.

`config/version.json` is called "the single source of truth" in four places
(`build.yml:389`, `docs/build.mjs:17`, `docs/contributing.md`) — but only for
**tool versions**. It has no `images` key. The tuple that actually defines a
published image — *(repo name, Dockerfile, stage, runner OS, test config,
registries)* — is written down nowhere, and re-derived by hand everywhere:

| # | Site | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `release.yml:36-39` | android, web |
| 2 | `release.yml:158-161` | android, web, **windows** ✓ |
| 3 | `release.yml:194-195` | android, web — **✗ windows** |
| 4 | `release.yml:242-243` | android, web — **✗ windows (#506)** |
| 5 | `build.yml:52-55` | android, web |
| 6 | `build.yml:230-233` | android, web |
| 7 | `build.yml:303-304` | android, web |
| 8 | `build.yml:456` | android hardcoded |
| 9 | `ci.yml:21` | android only (`env`) |
| 10 | `prepare-release.yml:32` | android only (`env`) |
| 11 | `cleanup-pr-image.yml:26` | android only (`env: PACKAGE_NAME`) |
| 12 | `windows-image.yml:39` | windows only (`env`) |
| 13 | `docs/build.mjs:47` | android, web, windows |
| 14 | `docker-compose.yml` | keyed by *stage*, no `flutter-` prefix |
| 15 | `openspec/specs/**` | says `release-android`; code says `release-linux` |

The same concept is spelled `matrix.name`, `env.IMAGE_REPOSITORY_NAME`,
`env.PACKAGE_NAME`, a JS array, and a compose service key.

**Two further instances of the identical defect, found during this
exploration and not yet filed:**

- `cleanup-pr-image.yml:26` hardcodes `PACKAGE_NAME: flutter-android`, but
  `build.yml:132-135` pushes `pr-<N>` GHCR tags for **both** Linux images.
  `flutter-web` PR tags therefore accumulate forever and are never deleted.
- `release.yml:151` gates `verify-published` on `github.event_name == 'push'`,
  while `openspec/specs/windows-image-release/spec.md:63-84` requires
  `workflow_dispatch` to rebuild Windows only. On a Windows-only dispatch,
  verification is skipped entirely — and if that guard were relaxed, its
  unconditional 3-leg matrix (`:158-161`) would fail the two Linux legs.

### 4. The structural seam that is missing

`windows-image.yml` is the repo's only `workflow_call` workflow
(`windows-image.yml:7`, called from `windows.yml:19` and `release.yml:131`),
and **it declares zero `outputs:`**. `jobs.build` (`:35`) has `env:` but no
`outputs:` block. So there is nothing downstream can `needs:`-and-read about
the Windows image — anything post-publish must re-derive its name from thin
air. `verify-published` works only because someone remembered to type
`flutter-windows` at `release.yml:161`.

`release-linux` (`release.yml:22`) is named after the **host OS**, not the
product, and publishes two products. So `needs: release-linux`
(`release.yml:186`, `:234`, `:285`) actually means "needs the job that happens
to be matrixed" — which is mechanically how `record-image` acquired its blind
spot.

The repo already articulates the correct principle in a different context.
`openspec/specs/ci-runner-disk-cleanup/spec.md:9`:

> The action SHALL dispatch its cleanup logic by `runner.os` internally;
> workflow YAML SHALL NOT branch on OS to choose between action paths.

`release-linux` / `release-windows` is precisely workflow YAML branching on
OS. And Windows is only *structurally* special in two ways — it needs

## Verdict up front

The issue asks a yes/no question — "verify whether Scout produces meaningful
output for the Windows image" — and the answer is **no, on three independent
grounds**. Scout is the wrong tool for `flutter-windows`, and no drop-in
replacement exists either. Adding `flutter-windows` to the `record-image`
matrix would produce a red or empty leg, not coverage.

But the issue's framing ("the same matrix-omission pattern as
`update-description`") is the more important half, and it is correct. #506 is
the third known instance of one structural defect, and a fourth was found
during this exploration. The defect is worth fixing even though *this*
symptom turns out to be a documentation task rather than a code task.

## Context

`record-image` (`.github/workflows/release.yml:227-276`) runs
`docker/scout-action` with `command: environment, cves` against
`registry://<owner>/<name>:<tag>`, then uploads SARIF to GitHub code scanning
with a per-image `category` (`release.yml:273-275`). Its matrix
(`release.yml:241-243`) lists `flutter-android` and `flutter-web`; it declares
`needs: release-linux` (`release.yml:234`).

```

        │
        ├──▶ release-linux ──────────┐  matrix [android, web]   release.yml:35-39
        │     (NO outputs:)          │
        │                            │
        └──▶ release-windows ─┐      │  uses windows-image.yml   release.yml:123-140
              (NO outputs:)   │      │
                              │      │
        ┌─────────────────────┴──────┴──────────┬──────────────┐
        ▼                    ▼                  ▼              ▼
  verify-published    update-description   record-image   create-github-release
  needs:[linux,       needs: release-linux needs:         needs: release-linux
         windows]                          release-linux
   :158-161            :193-195             :241-243        :285
  [android,web,WIN]   [android,web] ✗win   [android,web] ✗win
        ✓ correct         ✗ gap #2            ✗ ISSUE #506
```

Every one of those four post-publish jobs re-states the image set by hand.
`verify-published` is the only one that got it right — and it did so for a
documented reason, in a comment that is effectively a post-mortem of #506
written before #506 was filed (`release.yml:143-147`):

> "Did it publish?" is read from the registry by an anonymous pull, never
> inferred from which release job succeeded — that coupling is what let this
> job drift before.

**(a) Architecture.** Docker's health-scores page states an image is scored
N/A when "the image architecture is not linux/amd64 or linux/arm64", with the
remediation "rebuild the image for a supported architecture"

actually-published artifact — pulling the config blob for
`docker.io/gmeligio/flutter-windows:3.44.9` from the registry API:

```
os: windows    arch: amd64    os.version: 10.0.26100.32690
```

construction.

patch state as Windows Update KB records, which no SBOM cataloger models.

**4. Structural cause.** `windows-image.yml` is the only `workflow_call` workflow and declares **zero `outputs:`** — nothing downstream can read what Windows published. And `release-linux` is named after the *host OS*, not the product, so `needs: release-linux` means "needs the job that happens to be matrixed." The repo already states the right principle elsewhere (`ci-runner-disk-cleanup/spec.md:9`: workflow YAML SHALL NOT branch on OS).

=== proposal.md ===
## Why

Carrying one value from `config/version.json` to a Docker build costs **five file
edits**: a `core.exportVariable` call in `script/setEnvironmentVariables.js`, plus
a `--build-arg` line in each of four copy-pasted blocks (`build.yml` push path
`:158-164`, `build.yml` fork path `:180-186`, `ci.yml:84-90`,
`release.yml:112-118`).

That cost has already caused a defect. `android.java.version` sits in the manifest
but reaches no build, so the shipped JDK is fixed by hand-typed strings in
`android.Dockerfile` while the manifest merely reports what a previous build
happened to contain. The field was left unwired because wiring it was expensive,
not because it shouldn't be wired.

The four duplicated blocks are also four opportunities to disagree about what was
built. They are kept in sync only by hand.

Relevance gate: this changes observable behaviour a CI engineer depends on — which
versions the published image is actually built with, and whether the four build
legs agree. It also removes the barrier that keeps a manifest field from
influencing the image it describes.

## What Changes

- `script/setEnvironmentVariables.js` gains a single declarative table mapping
  manifest paths to build-argument names, and derives its exports from that table
  instead of eleven hand-written `core.exportVariable` calls.
- The emitter produces one `BUILD_ARGS` value (newline-separated `name=value`
  pairs); the four copy-pasted blocks collapse to
  `build-args: ${{ env.BUILD_ARGS }}`.
- Existing build-argument names are **preserved exactly**. This is a refactor of
  authoring, not of the wire format.

Explicitly **not** a mechanical derivation from the JSON path. The established
names are not derivable: `android.cmake.version` → `cmake_version` drops a
segment, `windows.vsBuildTools.cmakeProject.version` → `vs_cmake_version`
abbreviates two, and `android.ndk.version` → `android_ndk_version` retains the
trailing `version` that a drop-the-suffix rule would remove. A rule that produced
a self-consistent set would rename every `ARG` in both Dockerfiles for no user
benefit. The honest artifact is a table.

Not in scope, and stated so it is not mistaken for an omission: the Windows image
build (it hand-assembles a PowerShell array rather than using
`docker/build-push-action`, so it needs a different shape); renaming any existing
build argument; and moving the nine Renovate-owned apt pins into the manifest.

## Capabilities

### New Capabilities

- `manifest-build-arg-wiring`: how `config/version.json` fields reach the Docker
  build — the declared name mapping, the single emission point, and the per-ARG
  granularity that keeps layer caching intact.

## Impact

**Modified**: `script/setEnvironmentVariables.js` (table-driven emitter +
`BUILD_ARGS`); `.github/workflows/build.yml` (two build-arg blocks),
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.github/workflows/release.yml` (one each).

**Unchanged by design**: every build-argument name and value; every `ARG`
declaration in `android.Dockerfile` and `windows.Dockerfile`;
`config/version.json` itself; `windows-image.yml`.

**Verification**: the emitted `--build-arg` set must be byte-identical to the
current one. Because no name or value changes, a diff of the resolved
`docker buildx build` command line before and after is a complete check.

**Risk**: `BUILD_ARGS` makes the four call sites opaque — a reader no longer sees
which arguments are passed. Mitigated by the job log printing the resolved value
and by the table being a single readable list. Net legibility improves: one
authoritative list replaces four hand-synced copies.

**Enables**: wiring `android.java.version` through to the image
(`flutter-java-version-derivation`), which is blocked on this cost today. That
change depends on this one only for convenience — it can declare its own ARG
either way.

1	## Context
2	
3	`script/setEnvironmentVariables.js` hand-lists eleven `core.exportVariable` calls;
4	four workflow files each restate the same six `--build-arg` lines. Adding one
5	manifest value means touching five files. Full findings in
6	`../loud-deb-pin-resolution/research.md` (F10).
7	
8	## Goals / Non-Goals
9	
10	**Goals:**
11	
12	- Adding a manifest value costs one table row plus one `ARG`, not five file edits.
13	- The four Linux build legs read one authoritative list and cannot drift.
14	- Per-ARG Docker layer-cache granularity is preserved exactly.
15	- Zero change to emitted build-argument names and values.
16	
17	**Non-Goals:**
18	
19	- Renaming any build argument.
20	- The Windows image build (`windows-image.yml:130-149` assembles a PowerShell
21	  array, not a `build-args:` block).
22	- Moving the nine Renovate-owned apt pins into `config/version.json`.
23	
24	## Decisions
25	
26	### D1 — A declared table, not a derivation rule
27	
28	The first design of this change specified mechanical derivation from the JSON path
29	(lowercase, underscore-separate, drop a trailing `.version`/`.build`). Checking it
30	against the eleven names actually in use showed it cannot work:
31	
32	| Manifest path | Actual ARG | Why no rule produces it |
33	|---|---|---|
34	| `android.ndk.version` | `android_ndk_version` | retains `version` |
35	| `android.cmake.version` | `cmake_version` | drops the `android` segment |
36	| `windows.git.version` | `git_version` | drops the `windows` segment |
37	| `windows.vsBuildTools.cmakeProject.version` | `vs_cmake_version` | abbreviates two segments, retains `version` |
38	| `windows.vsBuildTools.windows11Sdk.build` | `vs_win11sdk_build` | abbreviates two segments, retains `build` |
39	| `android.platforms` | `android_platform_versions` | array → space-joined string |
40	
41	Any single rule contradicts at least half of these. A rule that produced a
42	self-consistent set would rename every `ARG` in both Dockerfiles — a coordinated
43	multi-file change that no consumer of the image benefits from.
44	
45	So the table *is* the specification. It is smaller than the eleven hand-written
46	export calls it replaces, every exception is visible in one place rather than
47	implied by its absence, and it makes the "one row per value" cost explicit.
48	
49	### D2 — `BUILD_ARGS` as newline-separated pairs, not a serialized manifest
50	
51	`docker/build-push-action`'s `build-args:` input is already newline-separated
52	`name=value`, so emitting that exact shape means the four call sites become
53	`build-args: ${{ env.BUILD_ARGS }}` with no other change.
54	
55	**Layer caching is the constraint that shapes this.** The tempting simplification —
56	one JSON build-arg, or `COPY config/version.json` into the build — would make any
57	version change invalidate every layer below it. Builds run 15–25 minutes and lean
58	on registry buildcache (`build.yml:151-152`), so a Fastlane bump must not re-clone
59	the Flutter SDK. Emitting N pairs keeps BuildKit seeing N distinct build-args
60	exactly as today. Only *authoring* is centralized; the wire format is unchanged.
61	
62	### D3 — Non-manifest exports keep their own names
63	
64	`FLUTTER_VERSION` is read by tagging and test steps, not only by the build.
65	`IMAGE_REPOSITORY_PATH` is composed from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER` and
66	`IMAGE_REPOSITORY_NAME` and never appears in the manifest at all. Both continue
67	to be exported individually. `BUILD_ARGS` covers manifest-derived build arguments;
68	it is not a replacement for the environment.
69	
70	## Automated Test Strategy
71	
72	The change is a pure refactor with a complete, cheap check: **the resolved
73	`docker buildx build` command line must be byte-identical before and after.**
74	
75	1. Capture the current `--build-arg` set from a recent CI run's build step
76	   (run `31194164846` shows the present form).
77	2. After the refactor, compare the same line from a PR run — same names, same
78	   values, same count.
79	
80	Because no name or value changes, that diff is exhaustive; no new test
81	infrastructure is warranted. The existing `container-structure-test` legs
82	(`test/android.yml`) remain the backstop that the built image is correct.
83	
84	## Observability
85	
86	| Failure | Surfaces as |
87	|---|---|
88	| Table omits a value a Dockerfile declares | Empty `ARG` → build fails at the consuming `RUN` |
89	| Table names a path absent from the manifest | Emitter throws → the step fails before any build starts |
90	| `BUILD_ARGS` malformed (missing `=`) | `docker/build-push-action` rejects the input |
91	| A workflow still restates args inline | Caught in review; the delta forbids it |
92	
93	**Logging**: the emitter should print the resolved `BUILD_ARGS` so a job log shows
94	exactly what was passed. This is what preserves legibility once the four call
95	sites stop listing arguments individually.
96	
97	**Cannot fail silently**: a missing build argument becomes an empty `ARG`, and
98	every current consumer uses its value in a `RUN` that fails without it.
99	
100	## Risks / Trade-offs
101	
102	**[`BUILD_ARGS` is opaque at the call site]** → Four workflow files no longer show
103	which arguments are passed. Mitigated by logging the resolved value and by the
104	table being one readable list. Net legibility improves: four hand-synced copies
105	become one authoritative list.
106	
107	**[The table is still hand-maintained]** → It is, and deliberately. The
108	alternative is a rule that renames every `ARG`. One row per value, in one file, is
109	the honest floor for this manifest.
110	
111	**[Refactor touches four workflow files at once]** → Unavoidable, since the point
112	is removing duplication. Bounded by the byte-identical check: if the emitted set
113	matches, the refactor is correct.
114	
115	## Migration Plan
116	
117	1. Add the table and `BUILD_ARGS` emission to `setEnvironmentVariables.js`, keeping
118	   the existing per-name exports in place. Nothing consumes `BUILD_ARGS` yet, so
119	   this is inert and independently revertable.
120	2. Switch the four call sites to `build-args: ${{ env.BUILD_ARGS }}`, and verify
121	   the emitted set against the step-1 baseline.
122	3. Drop the per-name exports that nothing reads any more, keeping `FLUTTER_VERSION`
123	   and `IMAGE_REPOSITORY_PATH` (D3).
124	
125	Rollback: each step is a separate commit; step 2 is the only one that changes what
126	is passed to a build.
127	
128	## Open Questions
129	
130	1. **Does `windows.Dockerfile` eventually adopt this?** It would need a different
131	   emission shape (PowerShell array, not newline pairs). Out of scope here;
132	   revisit if the Windows leg migrates to `docker/build-push-action`.

Ordered by the migration plan in `design.md`: each group is independently
revertable, and only group 2 changes what a build receives.

## 1. Table-driven emitter (design D1, D2)

- [ ] 1.1 Capture the current `--build-arg` set as a baseline from a recent CI run's `docker buildx build` command line — six args with their values — to diff against after the refactor
- [ ] 1.2 Add the mapping table to `script/setEnvironmentVariables.js`: one row per manifest path → build-argument name, reproducing all current names exactly (`android.ndk.version` → `android_ndk_version`, `android.cmake.version` → `cmake_version`, `windows.git.version` → `git_version`, `windows.vsBuildTools.cmakeProject.version` → `vs_cmake_version`, `windows.vsBuildTools.windows11Sdk.build` → `vs_win11sdk_build`, `windows.vsBuildTools.vcTools.version` → `vs_vctools_version`)
- [ ] 1.3 Give `android.platforms` a declared transform in the same table (array of `{version}` → space-joined string), so the one non-scalar shape is visible rather than special-cased in code
- [ ] 1.4 Emit `BUILD_ARGS` as newline-separated `name=value` pairs via `core.exportVariable`, restricted to the Linux build's six manifest-derived arguments
- [ ] 1.5 Fail the emitter with a named error if a table row references a manifest path that does not resolve, rather than exporting an empty value
- [ ] 1.6 Log the resolved `BUILD_ARGS` so the job log shows what was passed once the call sites stop listing arguments (design D1 legibility mitigation)
- [ ] 1.7 Keep every existing per-name export in place for now — this group is inert and nothing reads `BUILD_ARGS` yet

## 2. Collapse the four call sites (design D2)

- [ ] 2.1 Replace the build-args block with `build-args: ${{ env.BUILD_ARGS }}` in `build.yml` push path (~:158-164), `build.yml` fork path (~:180-186), `ci.yml` (~:84-90), `release.yml` (~:112-118)
- [ ] 2.2 Verify the emitted `--build-arg` set is byte-identical to the 1.1 baseline — same six names, same values, same count, no behaviour change
- [ ] 2.3 Confirm no workflow file still contains an inline `flutter_version=` or `android_ndk_version=` build-arg line

## 3. Retire the superseded exports (design D3)

- [ ] 3.1 Grep the workflows for each per-name export (`FASTLANE_VERSION`, `ANDROID_BUILD_TOOLS_VERSION`, `ANDROID_PLATFORM_VERSIONS`, `ANDROID_NDK_VERSION`, `CMAKE_VERSION`) and confirm the build step was its only reader
- [ ] 3.2 Delete the exports that group 2 made redundant
- [ ] 3.3 Keep `FLUTTER_VERSION` (read by tagging and test steps) and `IMAGE_REPOSITORY_PATH` (not manifest-derived) — confirm by grep that both still have readers

## 4. Verification

- [ ] 4.1 `container-structure-test` passes `test/android.yml` against an image built through the new path
- [ ] 4.2 Confirm a warm-cache rebuild whose only manifest change is `fastlane.version` still serves the Flutter clone layer from cache (per-ARG granularity preserved, design D2)
- [ ] 4.3 Confirm the Windows leg is untouched — `windows-image.yml` still assembles its own PowerShell argument array

## 5. Wrap-up

- [ ] 5.1 Open the PR with a Conventional Commit title, one logical concern
- [ ] 5.2 Note in the PR that no build-argument name or value changed, and that the resolved command line was diffed against the pre-refactor baseline

content.text:
Having read the actual artifacts, **I'd revise my earlier sequencing note.** It was reasoning from "both touch the manifest, so serialize them" — but they don't overlap the way I implied.

## They're orthogonal, not stacked

The two changes move in **opposite directions through the same file**:

```
                    config/version.json
                            │
                    ┌───────┴────────┐
                    ▼                ▼
        setEnvironmentVariables.js   (C adds: images[])
                    │                       │
   MBAW: ───────────┤                       │
   collapse 11 exports                      │
   into BUILD_ARGS                          │
   (values FLOWING OUT,                     │
    per-image invocation)                   │
                    │                       │
                    ▼                       ▼
            build-args:              matrix: fromJSON(...)
            (build phase)            (job topology)
```

The decisive detail is `setEnvironmentVariables.js:15-18`: **`IMAGE_REPOSITORY_NAME` is a required *input*, not an output.** The chokepoint is deliberately image-agnostic — every caller tells it which image it's working on (`build.yml:64`, `release.yml:41`, `windows-image.yml:39`). MBAW keeps that shape exactly; it changes what comes *out* per invocation. C needs something that answers "which images exist" *before* any per-image invocation — a different question, answered at a different point in the run.

Concretely, MBAW's file-level footprint is `setEnvironmentVariables.js` (the export block, lines 28-50) plus four `build-args:` blocks. C's is a new `images` key, `config/schema.cue`, and the `strategy.matrix` blocks — **`build-args:` and `strategy.matrix` are different keys in the same YAML files.** Git-level conflicts would be incidental, not semantic.

## The real ordering constraint is elsewhere

C has a hard prerequisite MBAW doesn't supply and isn't blocked by: **`windows-image.yml` declares zero `outputs:`** (`:35`). Until it does, no post-publish job can fan out over what Windows published. That's C's actual gate.

So the natural order is:

```
  windows-image.yml outputs:     ← C's true prerequisite
            │
            ├─────────────┬──────────────┐
            ▼             ▼              ▼
      C: images[]    MBAW (parallel,  B: document
      in manifest     independent)     the Scout skip
```

## What I'd actually do

**Run MBAW first — but for scheduling reasons, not dependency reasons.** Three of them:

1. **It's in flight already** (18 tasks, `status: in-progress`). Finishing beats interleaving.
2. **It establishes the manifest-table convention** that C should imitate. MBAW's D1 decision — *"the table **is** the specification"*, rejecting mechanical derivation — is exactly the argument C needs for its `images` rows (`flutter-android` → `android.Dockerfile`/`android` stage/`ubuntu-24.04` is equally underivable). Landing MBAW first means C cites a precedent instead of relitigating it.
3. **It has a byte-identical verification check** (`design.md:72-73`) that C does not. Land the change with the cheap proof first, while CI is quiet.

But that's soft. If you'd rather start C now, **the one thing to do first is add `outputs:` to `windows-image.yml`** — small, independently useful (it fixes the `verify-published` hardcode at `release.yml:161` on its own), and unblocking regardless of MBAW's state.

One correction worth flagging: MBAW's Open Question 1 asks whether `windows.Dockerfile` eventually adopts the table. C makes that question sharper rather than answering it — a `runner` field in the `images` row is precisely what would let the emitter pick newline-pairs vs. PowerShell-array. Worth noting in C's design, though still out of scope for both.

content.text:
That changes the picture substantially — and in Option C's favor. What shipped isn't the `BUILD_ARGS` string from the proposal; it's a **composite action** that owns the whole build step.

## What actually landed (#540)

The design pivoted between the proposal I read and the merge:

| Proposal said | #540 shipped |
|---|---|
| `BUILD_ARGS` newline string from the emitter | Build args stay inline, in **one** place — the composite action |
| Collapse four `build-args:` blocks | Collapse four **whole build steps** into `.github/actions/build-linux-image` |
| — | Plus `.github/actions/validate-version-manifest` |
| Emitter throws on missing path | Shipped (`read()` helper, `core.setFailed`) |

The proposal's D2 (`BUILD_ARGS` as the wire format) was dropped. Better call — the composite action gets the same no-drift guarantee without the opacity risk D2 had to mitigate.

**Two things this establishes that Option C directly inherits:**

1. **The composite-action precedent is now the dominant one.** The repo has three composite actions (`clean-runner-disk`, `build-linux-image`, `validate-version-manifest`) and still exactly one reusable workflow. The action's own header states the rule: *"Composite, not a reusable workflow: the legs need job-local state that a job boundary would break."*

2. **A new spec exists** — `openspec/specs/linux-image-build-boundary/spec.md` (160 lines). C has to be consistent with it.

And one finding that lands right on #506's territory — from the action's header:

> Android-only on purpose. `windows.git.version` and the Debian `git` apt pin are both `GIT_VERSION` in the env, so a Windows arg here could route the wrong one.

**That's a namespace collision in the flat env, and it's a concrete argument for C.** The emitter flattens `windows.git.version` and the Debian pin onto one name; the fix was to exclude Windows from the shared action. An `images[]` entry carrying its own scope is what removes that hazard rather than routing around it.

## What I'd do now

Read the new spec and baseline first — C's design has to sit on top of them, and I've now been wrong once about assuming proposal ≈ merge.

**Then: `windows-image.yml` outputs, as its own small change.** That was C's prerequisite before #540 and still is; #540 didn't touch it (3 lines, just the validate-action call). It's independently useful — it fixes the `verify-published` hardcode at `release.yml:161` on its own merits.

**Then C proper**, which I'd now scope more narrowly than in the research doc. #540 already killed the build-phase duplication. What remains is the **post-publish** fan-out — `record-image` (#506), `update-description`, `cleanup-pr-image.yml`'s `flutter-web` tag leak. That's a tighter change than "declare the image set and derive every matrix," and it's the part #506 actually asked about.

1	# linux-image-build-boundary Specification
2	
3	## Purpose
4	
5	Define the boundary that makes the Linux (`android.Dockerfile`) image build a single callable unit — a composite action under `.github/actions/` that owns the `docker/build-push-action` invocation and every build argument, used by all four Linux build legs (`build.yml` push path, `build.yml` fork path, `ci.yml`, `release.yml`). Covers where build arguments are declared, how unresolvable manifest values fail before a build starts, and the per-argument caching that the boundary preserves. The experience context is the CI engineer who trusts that the image validated on a pull request is built the same way as the image published on release, and who waits on a build that should rebuild only what actually changed.
6	
7	## Requirements
8	
9	### Requirement: The Linux image build exists once, as a callable unit
10	
11	The step that builds the Linux image SHALL be defined once, as a composite action
12	under `.github/actions/`. Every workflow step that builds `android.Dockerfile`
13	SHALL use it rather than restate the build inline.
14	
15	The callable unit SHALL own the `docker/build-push-action` invocation, including
16	the Dockerfile path and every build argument.
17	
18	Callers SHALL pass only the values in which their leg legitimately differs — the
19	build target, cache configuration, output mode, whether attestations are
20	produced, and the tags and labels from their own metadata step. A caller SHALL
21	NOT restate a build argument.
22	
23	The unit SHALL be a composite action rather than a reusable workflow, because a
24	reusable workflow is a separate job and the legs depend on job-local state:
25	`ci.yml` builds with `load: true` into the local Docker daemon and tests it in a
26	later step of the same job, and `build.yml` interleaves the build with
27	fork-handoff steps that share `steps.handoff` and `steps.metadata`. A composite
28	action runs inside the calling job, so that state is preserved.
29	
30	This follows the boundary the repository already uses for shared steps
31	(`.github/actions/clean-runner-disk`, used by every Linux leg).
32	
33	**Experience context:** A CI engineer trusts that the image validated on a pull
34	request is built the same way as the image published on release. Before this
35	requirement the same ~45-line build step was copy-pasted four times
36	(`build.yml` push path, `build.yml` fork path, `ci.yml`, `release.yml`) and had
37	already drifted: only `release.yml` passed `buildkitd-flags: --debug`, only
38	`release.yml` logged into Quay, `ci.yml` had no GHCR login, and only `build.yml`
39	requested attestations. Each divergence was invisible unless a maintainer diffed
40	four files by hand.
41	
42	#### Scenario: Every Linux build leg runs the same procedure
43	
44	- **GIVEN** the `build.yml` push path, the `build.yml` fork path, `ci.yml`, and `release.yml`
45	- **WHEN** a maintainer reads how each builds the image
46	- **THEN** each uses the shared Linux image build action
47	- **AND** no workflow file contains an inline `build-args:` block naming `flutter_version` or `android_ndk_version` for `android.Dockerfile`
48	
49	#### Scenario: A change to the build arguments reaches every leg
50	
51	- **GIVEN** a maintainer adds a build argument the image needs
52	- **WHEN** the change is made in the shared action
53	- **THEN** all four legs build with it
54	- **AND** no leg can be left behind, because no leg carries its own copy
55	
56	#### Scenario: Fork PR build receives the same arguments as a push build
57	
58	- **GIVEN** a pull request from a fork, which builds but cannot push
59	- **WHEN** the fork build path runs
60	- **THEN** it receives the identical build-argument set as the push path
61	- **AND** the two paths cannot drift, because they use one action
62	
63	#### Scenario: A leg's genuine difference is declared, not duplicated
64	
65	- **GIVEN** `ci.yml` uses the `gha` cache backend and produces no attestations, while `build.yml` uses the registry cache and does
66	- **WHEN** each uses the shared action
67	- **THEN** the difference is expressed as input values
68	- **AND** neither leg restates the build arguments to express it
69	
70	### Requirement: Build arguments are declared where the Dockerfile they feed is named
71	
72	The build arguments passed to `android.Dockerfile` SHALL be declared in the same
73	workflow that names that Dockerfile, and SHALL NOT be transported to it through a
74	shared environment value assembled elsewhere.
75	
76	A workflow that builds `android.Dockerfile` SHALL NOT name any build argument
77	belonging to the Windows image (`git_version`, `vs_cmake_version`,
78	`vs_win11sdk_build`, `vs_vctools_version`).
79	
80	Build-argument names SHALL be preserved exactly as currently declared. Renaming is
81	not in scope: each name is also an `ARG` in a Dockerfile, so a rename is a
82	coordinated multi-file change with no benefit to the person consuming the image.
83	
84	**Experience context:** A maintainer reading the build sees which arguments reach
85	which Dockerfile without following an indirection. This matters because
86	`config/version.json` holds values for two different images, and two of them
87	collide by name once flattened: `windows.git.version` is the Git for Windows
88	release (`2.55.0`), while `android.Dockerfile:10` declares `ARG GIT_VERSION` as a
89	Debian apt pin (`1:2.47.3-0+deb13u1`) for a different tool with a different
90	version grammar. Keeping each image's arguments in the unit that builds it
91	means the wrong value cannot be routed to the wrong build — and a mistake would
92	not be silent, since BuildKit only *warns* about a build argument no `ARG`
93	declares.
94	
95	#### Scenario: Windows values cannot reach the Linux build
96	
97	- **GIVEN** `config/version.json` contains both `windows.git.version` and the Linux image's values
98	- **WHEN** the Linux image is built
99	- **THEN** the build receives only the seven android build arguments
100	- **AND** no Windows-derived value appears on the resolved command line
101	
102	#### Scenario: Established names are preserved exactly
103	
104	- **GIVEN** the build moves into the shared action
105	- **WHEN** the resolved `docker buildx build` command line is compared to the previous one for the same leg
106	- **THEN** the build-argument names and values are identical
107	- **AND** no `ARG` declaration in any Dockerfile required an edit
108	
109	### Requirement: A manifest value that cannot be resolved fails before any build starts
110	
111	`script/setEnvironmentVariables.js` SHALL fail with a named error when a manifest
112	path it reads does not resolve, rather than exporting an empty or `undefined`
113	value. It SHALL log the values it resolved, so a job log records what was passed.
114	
115	**Experience context:** A maintainer who renames or removes a field in
116	`config/version.json` learns immediately, at the step that reads it, instead of
117	15 minutes later inside a Docker layer — or, in the worst case, not at all. The
118	worst case is real: the `web` stage (`android.Dockerfile:225`) declares none of
119	these arguments, so a wrong or empty value passed to a `web` build is silently
120	ignored rather than failing at a consuming `RUN`.
121	
122	#### Scenario: Unresolvable manifest path fails the step
123	
124	- **GIVEN** the emitter reads a path that `config/version.json` no longer contains
125	- **WHEN** the step runs
126	- **THEN** it fails with an error naming the path
127	- **AND** no image build starts
128	
129	#### Scenario: Resolved values are visible in the job log
130	
131	- **GIVEN** any workflow that reads the manifest
132	- **WHEN** the emitter step completes
133	- **THEN** the job log shows each manifest-derived value it resolved
134	
135	### Requirement: The callable unit preserves per-argument layer caching
136	
137	The shared action SHALL pass one `--build-arg` flag per value. The manifest
138	SHALL NOT be passed as a single serialized build argument, and
139	`config/version.json` SHALL NOT be `COPY`-ed into any build stage for the purpose
140	of supplying versions.
141	
142	**Experience context:** A CI engineer waiting on a build sees an unchanged tool
143	rebuild only when that tool's own version changed. Image builds take 15–25 minutes
144	and depend on registry build cache; collapsing the arguments into one value would
145	make every version bump invalidate every layer beneath it, so a Fastlane patch bump
146	would re-clone the Flutter SDK.
147	
148	#### Scenario: Unrelated version bump reuses cached layers
149	
150	- **GIVEN** a build whose only manifest change is `fastlane.version`
151	- **WHEN** the image is rebuilt with a warm cache
152	- **THEN** the Flutter clone layer is served from cache
153	- **AND** only the Fastlane layer and those after it are rebuilt
154	
155	#### Scenario: Build command carries discrete arguments
156	
157	- **GIVEN** any Linux image build
158	- **WHEN** the resolved `docker buildx build` command line is inspected in the job log
159	- **THEN** it contains one `--build-arg name=value` flag per manifest-derived value
160	- **AND** it contains no build argument whose value is a serialized JSON document

Covers where build arguments are declared, how unresolvable manifest values fail before a build starts, and the per-argument caching that the boundary preserves. The experience context is the CI engineer who trusts that the image validated on a pull request is built the same way as the image published on release, and who waits on a build that should rebuild only what actually changed.

## Requirements

### Requirement: The Linux image build exists once, as a callable unit

The step that builds the Linux image SHALL be defined once, as a composite action
under `.github/actions/`. Every workflow step that builds `android.Dockerfile`
SHALL use it rather than restate the build inline.

The callable unit SHALL own the `docker/build-push-action` invocation, including
the Dockerfile path and every build argument.

Callers SHALL pass only the values in which their leg legitimately differs — the
build target, cache configuration, output mode, whether attestations are
produced, and the tags and labels from their own metadata step. A caller SHALL
NOT restate a build argument.

The unit SHALL be a composite action rather than a reusable workflow, because a
reusable workflow is a separate job and the legs depend on job-local state:
`ci.yml` builds with `load: true` into the local Docker daemon and tests it in a
later step of the same job, and `build.yml` interleaves the build with
fork-handoff steps that share `steps.handoff` and `steps.metadata`. A composite
action runs inside the calling job, so that state is preserved.

This follows the boundary the repository already uses for shared steps
(`.github/actions/clean-runner-disk`, used by every Linux leg).

**Experience context:** A CI engineer trusts that the image validated on a pull
request is built the same way as the image published on release. Before this

already drifted: only `release.yml` passed `buildkitd-flags: --debug`, only

#### Scenario: Every Linux build leg runs the same procedure

- **GIVEN** the `build.yml` push path, the `build.yml` fork path, `ci.yml`, and `release.yml`
- **WHEN** a maintainer reads how each builds the image
- **THEN** each uses the shared Linux image build action
- **AND** no workflow file contains an inline `build-args:` block naming `flutter_version` or `android_ndk_version` for `android.Dockerfile`

#### Scenario: A change to the build arguments reaches every leg

- **GIVEN** a maintainer adds a build argument the image needs
- **WHEN** the change is made in the shared action
- **THEN** all four legs build with it
- **AND** no leg can be left behind, because no leg carries its own copy

#### Scenario: Fork PR build receives the same arguments as a push build

- **GIVEN** a pull request from a fork, which builds but cannot push
- **WHEN** the fork build path runs
- **THEN** it receives the identical build-argument set as the push path
- **AND** the two paths cannot drift, because they use one action

#### Scenario: A leg's genuine difference is declared, not duplicated

- **GIVEN** `ci.yml` uses the `gha` cache backend and produces no attestations, while `build.yml` uses the registry cache and does
- **WHEN** each uses the shared action
- **THEN** the difference is expressed as input values
- **AND** neither leg restates the build arguments to express it

### Requirement: Build arguments are declared where the Dockerfile they feed is named

The build arguments passed to `android.Dockerfile` SHALL be declared in the same
workflow that names that Dockerfile, and SHALL NOT be transported to it through a
shared environment value assembled elsewhere.

A workflow that builds `android.Dockerfile` SHALL NOT name any build argument
belonging to the Windows image (`git_version`, `vs_cmake_version`,
`vs_win11sdk_build`, `vs_vctools_version`).

Build-argument names SHALL be preserved exactly as currently declared. Renaming is
not in scope: each name is also an `ARG` in a Dockerfile, so a rename is a
coordinated multi-file change with no benefit to the person consuming the image.

**Experience context:** A maintainer reading the build sees which arguments reach
which Dockerfile without following an indirection. This matters because
`config/version.json` holds values for two different images, and two of them
collide by name once flattened: `windows.git.version` is the Git for Windows
release (`2.55.0`), while `android.Dockerfile:10` declares `ARG GIT_VERSION` as a
Debian apt pin (`1:2.47.3-0+deb13u1`) for a different tool with a different
version grammar. Keeping each image's arguments in the unit that builds it
means the wrong value cannot be routed to the wrong build — and a mistake would
not be silent, since BuildKit only *warns* about a build argument no `ARG`
declares.

#### Scenario: Windows values cannot reach the Linux build

- **GIVEN** `config/version.json` contains both `windows.git.version` and the Linux image's values
- **WHEN** the Linux image is built
- **THEN** the build receives only the seven android build arguments
- **AND** no Windows-derived value appears on the resolved command line

#### Scenario: Established names are preserved exactly

- **GIVEN** the build moves into the shared action
- **WHEN** the resolved `docker buildx build` command line is compared to the previous one for the same leg
- **THEN** the build-argument names and values are identical
- **AND** no `ARG` declaration in any Dockerfile required an edit

### Requirement: A manifest value that cannot be resolved fails before any build starts

`script/setEnvironmentVariables.js` SHALL fail with a named error when a manifest
path it reads does not resolve, rather than exporting an empty or `undefined`
value. It SHALL log the values it resolved, so a job log records what was passed.

**Experience context:** A maintainer who renames or removes a field in
`config/version.json` learns immediately, at the step that reads it, instead of
15 minutes later inside a Docker layer — or, in the worst case, not at all. The
worst case is real: the `web` stage (`android.Dockerfile:225`) declares none of
these arguments, so a wrong or empty value passed to a `web` build is silently
ignored rather than failing at a consuming `RUN`.

#### Scenario: Unresolvable manifest path fails the step

- **GIVEN** the emitter reads a path that `config/version.json` no longer contains
- **WHEN** the step runs
- **THEN** it fails with an error naming the path
- **AND** no image build starts

#### Scenario: Resolved values are visible in the job log

- **GIVEN** any workflow that reads the manifest
- **WHEN** the emitter step completes
- **THEN** the job log shows each manifest-derived value it resolved

### Requirement: The callable unit preserves per-argument layer caching

The shared action SHALL pass one `--build-arg` flag per value. The manifest
SHALL NOT be passed as a single serialized build argument, and
`config/version.json` SHALL NOT be `COPY`-ed into any build stage for the purpose
of supplying versions.

**Experience context:** A CI engineer waiting on a build sees an unchanged tool
rebuild only when that tool's own version changed. Image builds take 15–25 minutes
and depend on registry build cache; collapsing the arguments into one value would
make every version bump invalidate every layer beneath it, so a Fastlane patch bump
would re-clone the Flutter SDK.

#### Scenario: Unrelated version bump reuses cached layers

- **GIVEN** a build whose only manifest change is `fastlane.version`
- **WHEN** the image is rebuilt with a warm cache
- **THEN** the Flutter clone layer is served from cache
- **AND** only the Fastlane layer and those after it are rebuilt

#### Scenario: Build command carries discrete arguments

- **GIVEN** any Linux image build
- **WHEN** the resolved `docker buildx build` command line is inspected in the job log
- **THEN** it contains one `--build-arg name=value` flag per manifest-derived value
- **AND** it contains no build argument whose value is a serialized JSON document

# Pre-refactor baseline (task 1.1)

Captured 2026-08-09 from real CI runs, to diff each leg's resolved
`docker buildx build` command line against after the refactor.

**Do not use run `31194164846`** (referenced in the original design). It predates
PR #537 and shows only six build args.

## Build arguments — identical across every Linux leg

All seven, in this order:

```
--build-arg flutter_version=3.44.9
--build-arg fastlane_version=2.237.0
--build-arg android_java_version=17
--build-arg android_build_tools_version=36.0.0
--build-arg android_platform_versions=36
--build-arg android_ndk_version=28.2.13676358
--build-arg cmake_version=3.22.1
```

Manifest at `f006815` / `config/version.json`. `android_java_version=17` is the
value PR #537 wired; its presence is what makes this baseline current.

## Per-leg distinguishing flags

Source runs: `build.yml` → `31313920183` (PR event, `731d39d`);
`ci.yml` → `31314363759` (main, `f006815`).

| Leg | target | cache | output | attestations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `build.yml` push, android | `android` | `type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/gmeligio/flutter-android:buildcache` (+`mode=max` on `cache-to`) | `--push` | `provenance,mode=max` + `sbom` |
| `build.yml` push, web | `web` | `type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/gmeligio/flutter-web:buildcache` (+`mode=max`) | `--push` | `provenance,mode=max` + `sbom` |
| `ci.yml` | `android` | `type=gha` (+`mode=max` on `cache-to`) | `--load` | none |
| `build.yml` fork | `android` | not captured — see below | `--load` (artifact handoff) | none |
| `release.yml` | `android`, `web` | not captured — see below | `--push` | see below |

The cache ref is **per target** (`flutter-android` vs `flutter-web`), so
`cache-backend` alone is insufficient as an input — the ref must be derived from
the image name. Task 1.4 must account for this.

## Two legs not captured, and why

- **`build.yml` fork path** — requires a PR from a fork; none in recent history.
  Its build-args block is byte-identical to the push path in the source
  (`build.yml:181-188` vs `:158-164`), so the seven args are known; only the
  output mode differs. Verify at task 3.4 against the source, not a run.
- **`release.yml`** — the latest run (`31194203112`) is at `0bc825f`, which
  predates PR #537 and shows **six** args. Not a valid baseline. Its block is
  byte-identical to the others in the source (`release.yml:114-121`), so the
  expected set is the seven above. Verify at task 4.2 against the source, and
  against the first real release run after this lands.

This gap is why task 5.1's source-level grep matters: for two of the five legs it
is the only pre-merge check available.

## Post-refactor confirmation (run 31318147664, PR #540)

Run-level diff of the resolved `docker buildx build` command line, captured after
the switch. Both `build.yml` push legs:

| Leg | build-args | target | output | cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| web | 7, identical to baseline (order + values) | `web` | `--push` | `type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/gmeligio/flutter-web:buildcache` (+`mode=max`) |
| android | 7, identical to baseline (order + values) | `android` | `--push` | `type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/gmeligio/flutter-android:buildcache` (+`mode=max`) |

```
##[group]Versions read from config/version.json
FLUTTER_VERSION=3.44.9
...
##[endgroup]
```

All 11 jobs in the run succeeded, including `Test image` and `Scan image` for
both images — which confirms the fork-handoff outputs and the SBOM attestation
path still work through the shared action.

Still verified against source only, per the gaps noted above: the `build.yml`
fork path (needs a fork PR) and `release.yml` (runs only on release).

content.text:
All findings hold on main. Here's the scope, sharpened against what actually shipped.

## What #540 changed for Option C

**The build phase is done.** #540 collapsed four build legs into `.github/actions/build-linux-image` and ratified it in a 160-line spec. Option C as written in the research doc ("declare the image set, derive every matrix") is now **partly obsolete and partly forbidden**:

| C's original scope | Status after #540 |
|---|---|
| Collapse build matrices (`build.yml:52-55`, `:230-233`, `release.yml:36-39`) | **Obsolete** — the shared action already prevents drift |
| Post-publish matrices (`record-image`, `update-description`) | **Untouched** — still the live defect |
| Emit build args from a manifest table | **Forbidden** — see below |

That last row matters. The new spec at `linux-image-build-boundary/spec.md:70-74`:

> Build arguments … SHALL be declared in the same workflow that names that Dockerfile, and **SHALL NOT be transported to it through a shared environment value assembled elsewhere.**

This is a deliberate reversal of the proposal's D2 (`BUILD_ARGS`). Whatever C does, it must not route build arguments through an `images[]` structure — that's now spec-violating. C is confined to **job topology**, not build inputs.

The spec also documents the collision I flagged (`:86-93`): `windows.git.version` is Git for Windows `2.55.0`, while `android.Dockerfile:10` declares `ARG GIT_VERSION` as a Debian apt pin `1:2.47.3-0+deb13u1` — same flat env name, different tools, different version grammars. And BuildKit only *warns* on an undeclared arg, so a misroute would be silent.

## Revised scope: post-publish only

```
BUILD PHASE                    POST-PUBLISH PHASE
(#540 — done)                  (Option C — the remaining work)
┌──────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ build-linux-image    │       │ record-image      ✗ windows │ #506
│ action, 4 legs       │       │ update-description ✗ windows│
│ spec-ratified        │       │ cleanup-pr-image   ✗ web    │ tag leak
└──────────────────────┘       │ verify-published   ✓ (hand) │
                               └─────────────────────────────┘
   build ARGS: spec says            job TOPOLOGY: unowned
   "declare locally"                 nothing declares the set
```

Three findings confirmed still live on `main` at `05b2919`:
- `release.yml:186-187` — `update-description`, no windows
- `release.yml:236-237` — `record-image`, no windows (#506)
- `cleanup-pr-image.yml:26` — `PACKAGE_NAME: flutter-android`, so `flutter-web` PR tags leak
- `windows-image.yml` — still zero `outputs:` (C's prerequisite, untouched by #540)

## Recommended sequence

**1. `windows-image.yml` outputs** — small, standalone, unblocks everything else. Fixes the `verify-published` hardcode (`release.yml:169`) on its own merit.

**2. The `flutter-web` PR tag leak** — independent bug, no prerequisites, currently leaking. Doesn't need C at all.

**3. Option C (post-publish fan-out) + #506's documentation** — these merge naturally now. Once post-publish fans out over published images, `record-image` needs an explicit reason for excluding Windows, which is exactly the Option B content: `windows/amd64` unsupported, 5.90 GB over the 4 GB limit, no MSRC feed. The exclusion becomes a declared property of the image row rather than a silent matrix omission.

That's a genuinely better outcome than B alone — the skip gets *encoded*, not just commented.

One open question C must settle: whether the image set lives in `config/version.json` (my original suggestion) or somewhere separate. content.text:
A bug I found during the Phase 0 exploration and mentioned in the research doc — but never explained end to end. Here it is.

`.github/workflows/cleanup-pr-image.yml` deletes the throwaway GHCR tags a PR creates once that PR closes. Line 26 hardcodes what it cleans:

```yaml
PACKAGE_NAME: flutter-android
```

That name is then the only thing it ever asks the GitHub API about (`:66`, `:82`) — list versions of package `flutter-android`, delete the matching `pr-<N>` one.

But PR builds push tags for **both** Linux images. `build.yml` fans out over `flutter-android` and `flutter-web`, and its GHCR tag push is per-`matrix.name`. So each PR creates two `pr-<N>` tags and the cleanup deletes one:

```
PR #123 opens
   ├─▶ ghcr.io/gmeligio/flutter-android:pr-123
   └─▶ ghcr.io/gmeligio/flutter-web:pr-123

PR #123 closes → cleanup-pr-image.yml
   ├─▶ deletes flutter-android:pr-123  ✓
   └─▶ flutter-web:pr-123 ────────────── never touched, stays forever
```

So every PR that has ever run a build has left a `flutter-web:pr-N` tag behind in GHCR, accumulating since `flutter-web` was added.

It's the same defect as #506 — a place that enumerates the image set by hand and was never updated when the second image arrived — which is why I grouped it with them. But it's independent work: no prerequisite, no relation to Docker Scout, and it's leaking right now. That's why I put it second in the sequence rather than folding it into Option C.

Two caveats on my confidence. I verified line 26 and the API calls directly on `main` just now. The "both images get PR tags" half I'm carrying from the structure agent's report (`build.yml:132-135`) and haven't re-read myself since #540 shifted that file — worth confirming before filing. And I haven't checked GHCR to count actual orphaned tags, so "accumulating forever" is inference from the code, not an observation.

Want me to confirm both, and check what's actually sitting in GHCR?

file.content:
name: Cleanup PR image tag

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [closed]
  delete:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: cleanup-pr-image-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.event.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  cleanup:
    name: Cleanup PR image
    # On `delete` events, only act on branch deletions (not tag deletions).
    # `pull_request: closed` is always in scope.
    if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' || github.event.ref_type == 'branch' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      packages: write
      contents: read
    env:
      PACKAGE_NAME: flutter-android
    steps:
      - name: Harden runner
        uses: step-security/harden-runner@9af89fc71515a100421586dfdb3dc9c984fbf411 # v2.19.4
        with:
          egress-policy: audit

      - name: Compute target tag
        id: tag
        env:
          EVENT_NAME: ${{ github.event_name }}
          PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
          REF_NAME: ${{ github.event.ref }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [[ "$EVENT_NAME" == "pull_request" ]]; then
            target="pr-${PR_NUMBER}"
          else
            target="branch-${REF_NAME//\//-}"
          fi
          # Defense in depth: fail closed if the computed tag does not match
          # the documented handoff-tag regex. Release tags (`<version>`) and
          # `buildcache` MUST be unreachable from this code path.
          if [[ ! "$target" =~ ^pr-[0-9]+$ ]] && [[ ! "$target" =~ ^branch-[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$ ]]; then
            echo "::error::computed tag '$target' does not match handoff-tag regex; refusing to proceed"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "target=$target" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "Computed target tag: $target"

      - name: Resolve and delete GHCR version
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          TARGET_TAG: ${{ steps.tag.outputs.target }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          # The package is user-owned (gmeligio); /user/packages/... is the
          # authenticated-user endpoint. The workflow GITHUB_TOKEN can delete
          # because the package -> repo Actions Access role is Admin.
          version_id=$(gh api \
            "/user/packages/container/${PACKAGE_NAME}/versions" \
            --paginate \
            --jq ".[] | select(.metadata.container.tags[]? == \"${TARGET_TAG}\") | .id" \
            | head -n 1)

          if [[ -z "$version_id" ]]; then
            echo "tag not found, nothing to delete (tag='${TARGET_TAG}')"
            exit 0
          fi

          echo "Deleting version_id=${version_id} tag=${TARGET_TAG}"
          status=$(curl -sS -o /tmp/delete-body -w '%{http_code}' \
            -X DELETE \
            -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GH_TOKEN}" \
            -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
            -H "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28" \
            "https://api.github.com/user/packages/container/${PACKAGE_NAME}/versions/${version_id}")

          case "$status" in
            204)
              echo "Deleted ${TARGET_TAG} (version_id=${version_id})"
              ;;
            404)
              echo "Version ${version_id} already gone (404); treating as idempotent success"
              ;;
            *)
              echo "::error::DELETE returned HTTP ${status} for version_id=${version_id}"
              cat /tmp/delete-body
              exit 1
              ;;
          esac

    # One leg per published Linux image, both from android.Dockerfile: `target`

        env:

          IS_FORK: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository }}
          PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
          REF_NAME: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          echo "is_fork=$IS_FORK" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          if [[ "$IS_PR" == "true" ]]; then
            echo "tag=pr-$PR_NUMBER" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "tag=branch-${REF_NAME//\//-}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      # Buildx Step A pushes this single tag with SBOM + provenance
      # attestations. PR builds live on GHCR only; release publishing to
      # Docker Hub continues from `release.yml`, unchanged.
      - name: Load image metadata
        uses: docker/metadata-action@c299e40c65443455700f0fdfc63efafe5b349051 # v5.10.0

      # via `registry://...@<digest>` in `scan-image`, skipping the
      # layer-walk indexing step. Attestations also benefit downstream
      # consumers (verifiable provenance, queryable SBOM).
      - name: Build image (push to GHCR with attestations)

content.text:
Both halves confirmed, and the leak is real and measured.

## Verified

**Code path** — `build.yml:48-55` matrixes both images; `IMAGE_REPOSITORY_PATH` derives from `matrix.name` (`:64`); metadata-action (`:132-138`) emits `ghcr.io/<owner>/<matrix.name>:pr-<N>`; both legs push. `cleanup-pr-image.yml:26` hardcodes `PACKAGE_NAME: flutter-android` and queries only that package (`:66`, `:82`).

**GHCR reality:**

| Package | Orphaned handoff tags |
|---|---|
| `flutter-android` | **2** (`pr-533`, `pr-543` — both open PRs, expected) |
| `flutter-web` | **22** (`pr-513` … `pr-543`) |

So `flutter-android` is clean — the two present are live PRs that haven't closed yet. Every closed PR's `flutter-web` tag is still there, back to `pr-513`. That's 22 orphans, and it grows by one per PR.

One correction to what I said earlier: I described these as accumulating "since `flutter-web` was added." The oldest orphan is `pr-513`, so either that's when web PR tags started or older ones were cleaned some other way — I didn't establish which, and it doesn't change the fix.

Worth noting what this costs beyond storage: each orphan is a full image index with SBOM and provenance attestations attached (`build.yml:151-155`), not a bare tag.

## Fix

Two lines, mechanically:

```yaml
strategy:
  matrix:
    package: [flutter-android, flutter-web]
env:
  PACKAGE_NAME: ${{ matrix.package }}
```

The tag-regex guard (`:49-52`) and the 404-idempotency case (`:88-90`) already handle a package that has no matching tag, so a matrix leg with nothing to delete exits cleanly at `:71-73`.

The 22 existing orphans need a one-off cleanup — the workflow only fires on `pull_request: closed` and `delete`, so it will never revisit them. Per your memory note, `tags == []` filtering is unsafe here (these are OCI indexes with attestation children); deleting by resolved version ID for a specific `pr-N` tag, as the workflow already does, is the safe path.

This is independent of #506 and Option C. Want me to file it as an issue, or open the PR?

content.text:
That settles it. Here's what I verified and what's genuinely open.

## Verified

**1. The manifest is machine-written, not hand-written.** `update-version.yml:348-375` composes it from three job outputs via `jq` overlays onto a base checkout. Renovate has no rule targeting `version.json` (grep found none) — the pipeline owns it end to end.

**2. The overlay is `. + $block` — a top-level merge.** Adding an `images` key is *safe* under it: `. + $a` replaces only the keys present in `$a` (`android`, `fastlane`), so `images` carries forward untouched from the base canvas. This was my main worry and it doesn't materialize.

**3. Every current key is a tool version.** `#Version` (`schema.cue:41-57`) is composed entirely of `#SemverPatch` / `#SemverMinor` / `#SemverQuad` / `#PlatformVersion`. There is no non-version concept in the file. An `images` array would be the first.

**4. The validation boundary is already right for this.** Consumers use `.github/actions/validate-version-manifest`; producers keep inline `cue vet` (`update-version.yml:100`, `:204`, `:300`). Either way `#Version` gates every write, so a new `#Image` definition would be enforced on every path with no new wiring.

**5. The collision the new spec fenced off is a naming collision, not a file collision.** `linux-image-build-boundary/spec.md:86-93`: `windows.git.version` (`2.55.0`) and `android.Dockerfile:10`'s `ARG GIT_VERSION` (Debian pin `1:2.47.3-0+deb13u1`) collide *after being flattened into env vars*. The manifest already holds values for both images without a problem — it's the flat env namespace that's unsafe. So my earlier caution ("putting job-topology data in the same file risks re-creating the collision") was **wrong**: an `images` array consumed via `fromJSON` into a matrix never passes through that namespace.

## What's missing to verify

Three things, and only one is a real blocker.

**A. Does the spec forbid this? — needs a judgment call, not a lookup.** `spec.md:70-74` says build arguments SHALL NOT be transported "through a shared environment value assembled elsewhere." An `images` array feeding `strategy.matrix` isn't a build argument and isn't an env value — so it reads as out of scope. But that spec was written days ago to close a specific hazard, and I'd rather have you confirm the intent than infer it. **This is the one that should gate the design.**

**B. Whether `cue vet` accepts the array shape.** `#PlatformVersion` proves arrays of structs validate fine (`schema.cue:45`), so I expect yes — but I haven't run `cue vet` against a draft `#Image` definition. That's a five-minute empirical check, not a design risk.

**C. Whether the post-publish jobs can actually consume it.** `fromJSON` into `strategy.matrix` requires the value to come from a job output, so a `setup`-style job would have to read the manifest and emit it — and `windows-image.yml` still declares no `outputs:`. This is the same prerequisite already at the top of the sequence, just re-confirmed from a second direction.

## Where I land

The file is fine. The real question isn't *where* the image set lives — it's whether `version.json` should hold non-version data at all, and that's a naming question about the file, not a safety one. If it grows an `images` key, "version manifest" becomes the wrong name for it.

Worth putting to you directly as C's first design decision: `images` inside `config/version.json` (one file, one validator, one loader, overlay-safe) versus a sibling `config/images.json` (keeps the version manifest purely about versions, costs a second schema and a second read). I'd lean to the former — the loader and the CUE gate already exist, and a second file is a second thing to keep in sync — but it's your call, and it's the decision that shapes the rest of C.
